sections.heading: Solar Roof or Traditional Solar Panels: Are Solar Shingles Any Good for a Roof Replacement?

c.v: Solar shingles are good at one job: turning a roof that needs replacing into a solar roof that still looks like a roof.

runs.v: They generate renewable energy and electricity that lowers energy bills, and those energy savings help homeowners save money over time. The disadvantages are real. Solar shingles produce roughly 57 to 72 watts per shingle or tile, cost more per watt, and produce less power per square foot than a rack-mounted panel, per SolarReviews, EnergySage, and NREL, so they need about 44% more roof area for the same output; panels convert more sunlight into power, and solar shingles are generally less energy efficient, partly because they sit flush on the roof and build up heat without airflow underneath. Per-watt pricing puts solar shingles at roughly 1.5 to 2 times the cost of panels, and some cost guides put a full system at 100% to 150% more than a traditional solar panel array. Specialized solar roofing contractors are also more limited than panel installers, because the work needs both roofing and electrical expertise, and a solar-shingle reroof can take weeks, compared with hours to a day for a rack-mounted array on a sound roof.

c.v: Durability depends on precise installation and on the product.

runs.v: Because they are the roof surface, solar shingles take more direct wear than raised panels, so check that a product is listed to withstand fire, wind, and hail (UL 7103 for a building-integrated photovoltaic roof covering, UL 790 Class A fire, UL 2218 hail, ASTM D3161 wind); some solar shingles are rated for winds up to 130 mph. Solar shingles typically last about 20 to 25 years, and some products carry 25-year warranties, while rack-mounted panels can last 25 to 30 years.

faqs.q: What is a solar shingle and how does it differ from solar panels?

runs.v: A solar shingle is building-integrated photovoltaics, BIPV, where the photovoltaic material is the roof covering itself, while solar panels are building-applied photovoltaics, BAPV, rack-mounted hardware added on top of an existing roof, per the DOE Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy and IEA-PVPS. On a West Orange hillside Tudor or Llewellyn Park estate home it produces energy from a uniform roof surface rather than from visible racked panels.

faqs.q: Are solar shingles a good fit for a West Orange home near the reservations?

runs.v: They suit a West Orange home with adequate south- and west-facing roof area, a pitch of 2:12 or steeper, and a roof due for replacement, since solar shingles require a complete roof replacement when the existing roof is not in suitable condition. Reservation-edge shade off South Mountain and Eagle Rock and heavy street-tree canopy cut output on north and shaded slopes, so active solar shingles belong on the sun-exposed planes, with matching non-solar shingles elsewhere.

faqs.q: Can I install solar shingles on just part of my West Orange roof?

runs.v: A solar shingle system requires a full reroof rather than installation on an isolated section, because a solar shingle is the roof covering itself. Active solar shingles cover the south- and west-facing planes, while the remaining planes take matching non-solar shingles that provide weather protection and hold a uniform appearance across the whole roof.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to install solar shingles in West Orange, NJ?

runs.v: Yes for the solar part: the photovoltaic and electrical work carries its own building and electrical permits and inspection, while the underlying reroof on a detached one- or two-family home counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7. A historic landmark or a home in a private community such as Llewellyn Park can need extra design review, so confirm requirements with the Township of West Orange construction office and any community rules before work begins.

faqs.q: What New Jersey incentives and rebates apply to a West Orange solar shingle installation in 2026?

runs.v: New Jersey's main program is the NJ Board of Public Utilities' Successor Solar Incentive (SuSI) program, which supports solar installations including solar shingles with a fixed per-megawatt-hour SREC-II incentive over a 15-year term; a May 2026 Board order kept its ADI registration open until June 1, 2027 or until each capacity block fills, and net metering, a sales-tax exemption on Form ST-4, and a property-tax exemption for the solar installation on Form CRES also benefit New Jersey homeowners. No federal residential solar tax credit applies to a system completed after December 31, 2025, because the IRS does not allow the 30% Residential Clean Energy Credit for expenditures made after that date. Check the NJ Clean Energy Program for any current rebates and ask a tax professional about eligibility.
